cards.rueckseite: **CPP = MAP − ICP**; MAP = ⅔ diastolic + ⅓ systolic. Monro–Kellie: fixed intracranial volume. Pressure autoregulation keeps CBF constant over a range of about **MAP 50–150 mmHg**. Other regulators: viscosity, metabolism (flow–metabolism coupling), **PaCO₂** (strongest) and hypoxia (vasodilation).

cards.vorderseite: Secondary brain injury after TBI: main insults
cards.rueckseite:
- **Hypotension:** SBP < 90 mmHg roughly **doubles mortality**
- **Hypoxemia:** vasodilation, ↑ ICP
- **Fever:** metabolism +10% per °C
- **Cerebral edema:** peaks after several days, mainly cytotoxic
**Steroids are harmful** in TBI (CRASH trial).
**Jugular venous saturation (SjvO₂) < 50%** or **brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO₂) < 15 mmHg**.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 646 ("15%" in the book means mmHg). Many centers treat PbtO₂ < 20 mmHg.

cards.vorderseite: Brain death: prerequisites, clinical exam, apnea test
cards.rueckseite:
**Prerequisites:** known catastrophic CNS cause, no confounders (drugs, metabolic), temperature > 36 °C, SBP ≥ 90/100.
**Exam:** coma (GCS 3), absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, oculovestibular, gag and cough reflexes.
**Apnea test:** no breathing with **PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg or ≥ 20 mmHg above baseline**.
Ancillary tests (angiography, CTA, TCD, EEG, perfusion scintigraphy) if exam/apnea test incomplete.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 646–647. Book gives core temp > 34 °C for assessment and > 36.5 °C for apnea test.

cards.rueckseite: **Peaked T waves, ST depression**, T inversion, QT prolongation, U waves; also arrhythmias. Caused by catecholamine surge (neurogenic stunned myocardium / Takotsubo-like).

zeilen: Peaked T, wide QRS, flat P

cards.rueckseite:
Sinus bradycardia can be a sign of **raised ICP** (Cushing reflex: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing).
Symptomatic: **atropine**, transcutaneous pacing, dopamine or epinephrine. Mobitz II or 3rd-degree block: **transvenous pacemaker** even if asymptomatic.

zeilen: Drug of choice in **septic shock**; MAP/CPP augmentation

cards.vorderseite: Sodium nitroprusside vs. nitroglycerin in neurosurgical patients
cards.rueckseite:
Both are vasodilators that **raise ICP** (cerebral vasodilation) and are relatively contraindicated with intracranial hypertension.
**Nitroprusside:** arterial + venous; risk of **cyanide toxicity** (lactic acidosis, tachyphylaxis); treat/prevent with thiosulfate, hydroxocobalamin.
**Nitroglycerin:** mainly venous; risk of methemoglobinemia (treat with methylene blue).
Preferred for BP control: **labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine**.

cards.vorderseite: Venous air embolism: signs, detection, treatment
cards.rueckseite:
Risk: sitting position, open venous sinuses. **Most sensitive:** TEE > precordial Doppler (mill-wheel sound); **drop in end-tidal CO₂**.
Treatment: flood field with saline/wax bone, compress jugular veins, lower head, **left lateral decubitus (Durant)**, 100% O₂, aspirate via right atrial catheter, hyperbaric O₂. Mortality ~15%.

~30% of patients in post-resuscitation coma regain consciousness. Still comatose after **48 h**: only 2–7% recover; after 7 days essentially none (classic data). Post-hypoxic **myoclonus** is the typical seizure type.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 650. Modern prognostication is multimodal and done ≥ 72 h after rewarming.

cards.rueckseite:
**Peak ↑, plateau normal** → airway resistance (secretions, bronchospasm, kinked tube): suction, bronchodilators.
**Peak and plateau ↑** → compliance ↓ (pneumothorax, atelectasis, edema, abdominal distension, auto-PEEP).
**Peak ↓** → air leak.

PEEP improves oxygenation but reduces venous return and cardiac output and can **raise ICP** (impaired cerebral venous outflow), especially when lung compliance is good. Other complications: barotrauma, fluid retention. Use the lowest PEEP that achieves oxygenation; maintain CPP.

**ARDS:** PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 300 (Berlin: mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤ 100), bilateral **diffuse peripheral** infiltrates, no Kerley B lines, clear bases, **protein-rich** fluid, PCWP < 18. Causes: sepsis, aspiration, trauma, pancreatitis. Diuretics/steroids not proven.
**Cardiogenic:** perihilar, Kerley B lines, effusions, PCWP > 18.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 652–653. Neurogenic pulmonary edema can follow SAH/TBI.
CNBR Table 7.6. Neurogenic shock after cervical/high thoracic SCI: loss of sympathetic tone → hypotension with bradycardia.

zeilen: Mild tachycardia, no IV replacement needed

cards.rueckseite: Only ~20% of crystalloid stays intravascular → ~3× the volume of colloid needed. Colloid expands faster, but **no survival benefit**. **Hetastarch** (HES) → renal failure, coagulopathy; **dextran** → platelet inhibition, anaphylaxis. In TBI, **albumin increased mortality** (SAFE-TBI) and hypotonic fluids are avoided.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 660–661 (book: hetastarch no coagulopathy; outdated).

zeilen: Urticaria; IgA deficiency → anaphylaxis; washed products
Donor antibodies; ARDS-like, resolves in ~4 days
ABO mismatch: fever, back pain, hypotension, DIC; direct Coombs

cards.rueckseite:
Spontaneous bleeding < 10,000/µL. For **neurosurgery aim > 100,000/µL** (book: 50,000 with bleeding, 80,000 for surgery). One apheresis unit raises the count ~30,000.
Dysfunction (uremia, aspirin, vWD): **desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 µg/kg**: releases vWF; platelet transfusion for antiplatelet drugs only selectively. Aspirin effect lasts the **platelet lifespan (7–10 d)**.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 663–664. PATCH trial: platelet transfusion harmful in antiplatelet-associated spontaneous ICH without surgery.

cards.rueckseite: Type II: antibodies against **heparin–PF4** complexes, platelet fall > 50% after **5–10 days**, paradoxical **thrombosis**. Stop all heparin (incl. flushes); anticoagulate with **argatroban** (or bivalirudin, fondaparinux, DOAC). No platelet transfusion, no warfarin until platelets recover.

zeilen: Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, factor VII deficiency
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 664–665 (book wrongly lists PT ↑ in hemophilia A).

cards.rueckseite:
**II, VII, IX, X** + proteins **C and S**. Shortest half-lives: protein C and **factor VII** → early INR rise and transient **hypercoagulability** (bridge with heparin, warfarin skin necrosis).
Reversal in ICH: **4-factor PCC + IV vitamin K** (vitamin K alone takes 12–36 h; FFP slower, volume load).
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 665. Book recommends FFP; current guidelines prefer PCC.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Warfarin:** 4F-PCC + vitamin K 10 mg IV
- **Unfractionated heparin:** protamine (1 mg per 100 U in the last 2–3 h)
- **Dabigatran:** idarucizumab
- **Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban):** andexanet alfa or 4F-PCC
- **Thrombolysis (tPA):** cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen), tranexamic acid
cards.notiz: Greenberg 10th ed.; CNBR p. 665 lists heparin → protamine.

cards.rueckseite: PT ↑, aPTT ↑, bleeding time ↑, **platelets ↓, fibrinogen ↓** (fibrinogen correlates best with bleeding), D-dimers ↑. Causes: sepsis, hemolytic transfusion reaction, malignancy, **severe TBI** (brain tissue factor). Treat the cause; replace platelets, **cryoprecipitate** (fibrinogen), FFP.

zeilen: Renal Na loss (natriuretic peptides, ↓ sympathetic drive)
**Fluid restriction**, salt tablets, 3% saline if severe
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 668. In SAH, hyponatremia is most often CSW; fluid restriction raises vasospasm/infarction risk.

cards.rueckseite:
**Central DI:** after pituitary/hypothalamic surgery, trauma, brain death, meningitis. Polyuria (> 250–300 mL/h), **urine osm < 200 mOsm/L, urine SG < 1.005**, serum Na and osm ↑.
Nephrogenic DI: lithium, aminoglycosides, amphotericin (urine osm 200–500).
Treatment: replace free water; **desmopressin (DDAVP)** for central DI. Triphasic response after pituitary surgery: DI → SIADH (days 6–10) → permanent DI.

Severe symptomatic (seizures, coma): **3% saline** bolus (e.g. 100–150 mL) to raise Na by 4–6 mmol/L quickly. Chronic: no more than **8–10 mmol/L per 24 h** to avoid **osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis)**; high risk in alcoholics, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease. Hypernatremia: correct over 48–72 h (cerebral edema).
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 668 (book: max 0.5 mEq/L/h). Current limits per European/US guidelines.

cards.rueckseite:
1. **Stabilize membrane:** calcium gluconate 10% 10–20 mL IV (not with digoxin toxicity)
2. **Shift into cells:** insulin 10 U + glucose, β2 agonist, NaHCO₃ if acidotic
3. **Remove:** furosemide, cation exchanger, **dialysis**
Avoid **succinylcholine** in denervation (SCI, stroke, burns, immobilization): massive K⁺ release.

cards.text: Anion gap = {{c1::Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)}}, normal {{c2::7–12 mEq/L}}. High-gap causes: {{c3::lactate, ketones, renal failure, salicylates, methanol, ethylene glycol}}.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 666. Hypoalbuminemia lowers the gap (~2.5 per 1 g/dL albumin).

cards.text: Winter's formula, expected PaCO₂ in metabolic acidosis = {{c1::1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (± 2)}}; in metabolic alkalosis ≈ {{c2::0.7 × HCO₃⁻ + 20}}.

cards.rueckseite: Hypotension (refractory to pressors), **hyponatremia, hyperkalemia**, hypoglycemia, pigmentation (primary). Diagnosis: ACTH (cosyntropin) stimulation test. Treatment: **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV**, then 50–100 mg q6–8 h (dexamethasone if test still pending). Relevant after pituitary surgery and chronic steroid use; **etomidate** suppresses cortisol synthesis.

cards.vorderseite: Cushing syndrome: causes and dexamethasone tests
cards.rueckseite:
Non-iatrogenic causes: **Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma) ~65%**, adrenal tumor ~25%, ectopic ACTH (small cell lung cancer, carcinoid) ~15%.
ACTH low → adrenal; high → pituitary or ectopic. **High-dose dexamethasone suppresses pituitary** Cushing but not ectopic or adrenal. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling for confirmation.

**MEN1 (Wermer):** parathyroid, pancreas, **pituitary** ("3 P").
**MEN2A (Sipple):** medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia.
**MEN2B:** medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus.
All autosomal dominant.

cards.vorderseite: Anesthetic agents: effect on CBF and CMRO₂
cards.rueckseite:
**Increase CBF/ICP:** volatile agents (halothane > enflurane > isoflurane/sevoflurane), **ketamine**, **nitrous oxide** (also ↑ CMRO₂; avoid with pneumocephalus).
**Decrease CBF and CMRO₂:** barbiturates (thiopental), propofol, **etomidate** (preserves BP, suppresses adrenal axis), opioids (fentanyl).
Enflurane lowers the seizure threshold.

Most common organism: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**, usually within 72 h (may occur years later with a persistent leak). Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended; pneumococcal vaccination is considered.

**SIRS** (≥ 2): T > 38 or < 36 °C, HR > 90, RR > 20 or PaCO₂ < 32, WBC > 12,000 or < 4,000 (or > 10% bands).
**Sepsis-3 (current):** life-threatening organ dysfunction (**SOFA ≥ 2**) due to infection. **Septic shock:** vasopressors to keep MAP ≥ 65 **and** lactate > 2 mmol/L despite fluids.

Day 1–2: **atelectasis** (usually no extensive workup). Day 3–5: urinary tract infection, pneumonia, line infection, DVT/PE. **Wound infection: days 5–7**. Neurosurgery: also consider meningitis/ventriculitis, drug fever, central fever (diagnosis of exclusion).
